round1.summary:
GRAIL is a three-stage rule-grounded metabolite structure predictor (learned rule selector over 7,581 SMIRKS templates, RDKit application, learned pair filter, reciprocal-rank fusion) submitted with an unusually disciplined evaluation: five matching criteria and nine output budgets swept, paired substrate bootstraps, fifteen pre-registered predictions with thresholds and falsification conditions, a numeral-provenance system tying every figure in the text to a pinned artifact, and a coverage census bounding what the rule bank can reach. The paper declines to claim a winner and reports where it loses.

I reviewed it as the methods and statistics referee, and checked the load-bearing numbers against the pinned artifacts under results/ that the review packet makes readable. The evaluation design is genuinely better than this literature's norm and the writing is candid to a degree I rarely see. But the three claims that carry the abstract do not survive checking as written, and in each case the disconfirming evidence is in the authors' own artifacts.

The 475-reference coverage bound is reported under one hydrogen-handling convention out of at least three the authors measured; the arms span 0.7351 to 0.8229 in coverage, i.e. 688 to 460 uncovered references, with the paired difference between the two naive arms at -0.0812 [-0.0957, -0.0679]. The word "hydrogen" appears nowhere in the manuscript. The abstract nonetheless calls the bound "a property of the annotation corpus rather than of our implementation" on the strength of invariance to an unrelated axis (the definition of a transformation type), while the axis that actually moves it by up to 213 references is an implementation choice, is undeclared, and — per results/ceiling_convention_matched.json — differs between the deployed path and the released public API, so a third party reproducing the ceiling from the released code gets the other number.

The k=30 lead rests on a population where GRAIL's ranking rule was selected. Section 2.4 states plainly that the fusion "was chosen among four" on the comparison set and measures the selection optimism for that contrast at 0.109 versus 0.0733. The only marginal lead in the paper, exhaustive versus MetaTox at k=30, is +0.038 [+0.005, +0.072] — smaller than the paper's own estimate of the optimism on that same population. The comparators were not tuned there.

The reproducibility claim is contradicted inside the submission: the Introduction says "the artifacts sufficient to recompute any cell are released" while SI Section S1 says "a third party can reproduce the tautomer column of Table S4 and not the rest of it," and four load-bearing items in the Data Availability Statement are unfilled placeholders.

Beneath these, three further defects bear on whether the numbers mean what the sentences say: all recall figures come from a single checkpoint with the only training-variance estimate being n=3 at a non-comparable operating point; the comparison population's provenance in the manuscript disagrees with the artifact behind Figure 1; and every one of the six cross-references from the main text into the SI points at the wrong table, which in a paper selling checkability is not a cosmetic matter.

None of this requires new science. It requires declaring a fourth axis the authors have already measured, sweeping the ranking selection the way the criterion is already swept, reporting seed spread at the deployed operating point, correcting the population description, filling the placeholders, and rewriting an abstract that currently overstates two of its three claims. That is a major revision, and I would expect the revised paper to be publishable here as the evaluation contribution it says it is.
round1.strengths:
The evaluation design is the contribution and it is a real one. Treating the matching criterion and the output budget as declared axes rather than defaults, and reporting the full 5-by-9 grid rather than a chosen cell, is the correct response to a literature where, as the paper shows on its own numbers, "the margin between GRAIL's better arm and the strongest comparator runs from -0.0692 under canonical SMILES equality to +0.0617 under the full InChIKey, a range of 0.1309, and the sign of the conclusion changes with it." I have not seen that demonstrated this cleanly in this field, and the multiverse framing (refs 23-24) is the right one.

The paper argues against itself in several places where it did not have to. It reports that its chosen criterion "sits 3 of 5, exactly the median" among criteria ordered by how many budgets each yields a lead. It measures the parent-drop convention it declared rather than assuming it, and reports that the largest effect is 0.003 across 45 cells. It reports that its own earlier ranking experiment "could not have answered" because "for 887 of 1,170 substrates the entire pool fits inside the budget, so every ordering returns the same set" — a self-invalidation most authors would quietly drop. SI S13's rule that "a ranking comparison carries information only over the substrates whose pool exceeds the budget, and the number of such substrates should be reported with the result" is a genuine methodological contribution that this literature needs.

The registered predictions are handled better than the norm. Nine of fifteen are reported, three of them failures with the failure mechanism diagnosed (P6's deficit split into -0.0647 from design and -0.0556 from model; P7 closed by an oracle rather than by model quality); the six unreported ones are stated with their thresholds so a later result cannot be a post hoc bar. The stricter interval reading is given alongside the as-written verdict: "P1, P2 and P5 each have a threshold inside their own interval, so the data establish that the effect exceeds zero and not that it exceeds the registered bar." That distinction is exactly right and almost never made.

The paired substrate bootstrap is the correct estimator for the question, and the reason given is correct: "Resampling substrates rather than predictions is what makes the interval one on the difference between two arms read on the same items." Refusing to order systems by precision under positive-unlabelled annotation, while printing it because it orders them differently, is the right call and is justified rather than asserted.

The ablations are unusually well controlled. Re-ranking one fixed pool five ways with no model runs isolates the combination form from the components. The group-ranking oracle is read against a size-matched random partition rather than against the deployed ranking, so that "a finer partition wins at an oracle for nothing" is controlled — and under that control molecular formula does not separate (-0.0030) while transformation type does (+0.0496). The learned-rule-choice ablation against the 30 highest-frequency applicable rules is the hard baseline, not the easy one, and the paper reports the modest +0.0316 [+0.0101, +0.0547] result as modest.

The coverage census is careful where it could have been rhetorical: the retrosynthetic-template control reports that "bank and library share 308 types, so the intersection measures real absence rather than two incomparable formalisms," and the Tanimoto-to-substrate baseline that needs no training is exactly the baseline a learned re-ranker must beat and that this literature does not report.

Finally, the honesty about what cannot be done is worth the venue. The contamination direction is stated ("their knowledge therefore overlaps our test substrates by construction, in a direction that flatters them"); the absence of an external set is explained structurally rather than excused; the 2025-26 wave is enumerated with the specific reason each could not be run; and the conclusion that "a reader therefore cannot presently verify any ranking in this literature" is the correct diagnosis and the correct case for releasing per-item predictions.
round1.venue_notes:
GROUNDING. JCIM Author Guidelines (researcher-resources.acs.org/publish/author_guidelines?coden=jcisd8, last updated 3 Jul 2026) put the journal at ACS Research Data Policy Level 2: a Data Availability Statement is required at submission, and the journal "encourages authors to publicly share all the data underlying the results." The software policy is stricter than most venues: software must be "generally available for evaluation or purchase at the time of publication," must be "made available for testing by reviewers," and "the name of the application being described should be clearly stated in the manuscript title." Scope is methodology in chemical informatics and molecular modeling, explicitly including machine learning on chemical data. The guidelines' own success criteria matter here: papers are "More Likely to Succeed" when they present "New approaches for modeling... benchmarked against multiple different tasks and consistently show superiority," and "Less Likely to Succeed" when they present "New approaches... without benchmarking, or if benchmarked, showed results similar to existing methods." Figures: 300 dpi colour, single column up to 3.33 in, double column 4.17-7 in, minimum 4.5 pt lettering. Articles have no hard word limit (unlike Letters at ~3500 and Application Notes at 5000), though ACS returns over-long manuscripts for editing before review. Public sources put JCIM's impact factor around 5.3 and Q1 in cheminformatics; I could not confirm an acceptance rate from any public source and do not rely on one.

HOW THIS BEARS ON THE SUBMISSION. Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions.

First, judged as a method paper this submission sits below the bar the guidelines state. It does not claim superiority — "The comparison does not produce a winner and we do not present one" — and its only clean lead is at k=30 and k=50, budgets at which, by its own accounting, "291 of MetaPredictor's lists, 249 of MetaTox's and 282 of the interactive arm's are shorter than the budget." An editor reading the guidelines literally would note that "results similar to existing methods" is the stated ground for decline.

Second, judged as an evaluation-and-diagnosis paper it is above the bar, and JCIM demonstrably publishes that genre. Two recent JCIM Articles set the calibration. Jacob et al., "Site-of-Metabolism Prediction with Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification," JCIM 2025, 65, 8462-8474 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.5c00762), from the Kirchmair group, is a metabolism paper whose contribution is a "comprehensive evaluation... identifying key challenges that currently constrain the performance of SOM prediction models" plus "actionable insights" — a rigor paper, not a leaderboard win. Gao et al., "Benchmarking In Silico Metabolite Prediction Tools against Human Radiolabeled ADME Data," JCIM 2026, 66, 2918-2928, is the submission's own reference 14 and is a pure comparison paper. So the declared-axes sweep, the registered predictions, the per-item prediction release and the coverage census are all within scope and are, on evidence, more careful than what this literature normally does. (Per PubMed: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.5c00762.)

The editorial consequence is that the decision turns on whether the paper's own headline claims survive. They are three: the k=30/k=50 lead, the 475-reference bound, and the release of "the artifacts sufficient to recompute any cell." I find all three defective as stated, and all three repairable from material the authors already hold. That is the shape of a major revision at this journal rather than a reject.

Two compliance points for the editor. The title, "Rule-grounded metabolite prediction under a fully declared evaluation," does not contain "GRAIL", which the software policy requires for a paper describing an application. And the Data Availability Statement carries four unresolved placeholders at submission ([ZENODO DOI], [CORPUS LICENCE], [CORPUS ASSEMBLY], [CURATED RULES]); under Level 2 the statement must be complete at submission, and here the missing items are precisely what the paper's central claim rests on. The manuscript runs about 6,600 words of body text (roughly 8,950 including tables, captions and references) with 5 tables and 4 figures, plus a 20-page SI with 9 tables — long for a JCIM Article but not out of range.

round1.summary:
GRAIL is a three-stage metabolite structure predictor — a 7,581-template SMIRKS bank, a learned rule selector, RDKit application, and a learned pair filter fused by reciprocal rank — evaluated against SyGMa, MetaTox and MetaPredictor on 291 shared substrates under five matching criteria and nine output budgets, with paired bootstrap intervals, a preregistration, and a coverage-ceiling analysis bounding the approach at 0.8171 of test references in one template application.

The evaluation contribution is real and, in my judgement, the best thing in this literature at present. The paper does what it says: it declares the two axes (matching criterion, output budget) that published comparisons leave unstated, sweeps both, reports intervals rather than levels, states where no ordering is established, and reports its own registered failures (P6, P7, P8) alongside its successes. Section 3.5 and Table S6, which show the sign of the conclusion flipping between canonical-SMILES and full-InChIKey matching at k=15, are the single most useful pages here and would change how I read every recall figure in this field. The claim discipline the authors set themselves is largely honoured.

The chemistry is where it falls short, and the shortfall is not cosmetic. I checked the released bank directly. Three findings bear on claims in the paper's own showcase. (i) The bank's curated core demonstrably contains a comparator's published rule set — the authors' own script `scripts/bank_overlap_sygma.py` measures 152 of SyGMa's 175 rules as verbatim members of GRAIL's curated subset, and its docstring asks whether the ceiling comparison is "between two banks or between a bank and a near-subset of itself." Neither the manuscript nor the SI says this, while both carefully disclose the opposite-direction contamination that flatters the comparators. (ii) The worked example's single interactive-mode hit depends on an undeclared axis: rule 4913 does not fire on gemcitabine as normally drawn and fires only on the minor 4-imino/2-hydroxy tautomer, so substrate tautomer canonicalisation — never swept, never declared — controls which rules fire at all. (iii) The three "phosphorylation" rules are one over-general template, LHS `[#6:1]-[#8:2]`, at three chain lengths; the di- and tri-phosphate templates each perform two and three enzymatic steps in one application with a *connected* reaction centre, which the SI's 8.9% composite measurement counts pieces and therefore cannot see, so "8.9% is an upper bound on the composite share" is falsified by the paper's own flagship molecule.

Add to that: the arm carrying every headline claim fails to finish within 600 s on roughly a tenth of substrates (11 of 106 in `results/cost_envelope.json`), a number that appears nowhere; GLORYx is runnable and ranked and is not a comparator; and the 475-metabolite gap is never named in chemical terms. The paper is above the JCIM bar on method and evidence and below it on chemistry, and the gap is closable with work the authors have already tooled.
round1.strengths:
The declared-axes framing is correct and overdue. "A recall figure depends on at least two settings that papers in this area report apart from their rankings or not at all: the rule deciding when a predicted structure counts as the reference, and the number of candidates a system may emit." That is exactly right, it is the reason the Boyce, Scholz and Gao comparisons keep reaching different verdicts, and Table S6 proves the point on the authors' own numbers rather than about someone else's: at k=15 the margin runs from -0.0692 under canonical SMILES to +0.0617 under the full InChIKey. I would want that table's discipline adopted as a norm.

The paper repeatedly declines advantages it could have taken. It reports that "the tautomer-aware key sits 3 of 5, exactly the median" among criteria ordered by how many budgets each yields a lead. It refuses to order systems by precision because "under incomplete annotation an unannotated but real metabolite counts as a false positive," and then prints precision anyway in Table S4 because it orders the systems differently. It states the contamination that flatters its comparators, in two places, unprompted. It reports three failed registered predictions with their measured deficits, and reports that three of its six confirmations are "unresolved rather than clear" on the stricter reading against the interval. Section S13 ("a ranking comparison carries information only over the substrates whose pool exceeds the budget") is a genuinely useful methodological result derived from the authors' own failed experiment.

The parent-drop sweep (Table S3) is the kind of check almost nobody runs: a convention that was declared but not measured, swept across 45 cells, with the two substrates whose own tautomer key is among their annotated references identified as the cause of the negative cells. The provenance machinery — 50 pinned artifacts, producer-hash invalidation, a split manifest pinning the triple files and the rule bank by digest, and the explicit statement that 117 of 269 files under `results/` carry no stamp and support no number — is better than anything I have refereed in this journal.

The chemistry that is present is honest where it matters. Section S9 concedes that "the coverage ceiling is a one-template ceiling" and that the depth-two experiment "measures a second template application rather than a second enzymatic step," and it records an abandoned instrument ("Parsing partially mapped SMIRKS is the wrong instrument for this question and its answer disagreed with what the molecules show") rather than quietly replacing it. The retrosynthetic-template control, with its shared-308-types check "so the intersection measures real absence rather than two incomparable formalisms," is well designed even though I think it answers the wrong question.
round1.venue_notes:
JCIM (ACS, IF 6.4 in the 2026 release, Q1, CiteScore 8.8, ~1,065 papers/yr, median peer review ~3 months, characterised publicly as "very difficult" for acceptance; no acceptance rate is disclosed by ACS). Scope: "papers reporting new methodologies in chemical informatics and molecular modeling and its applications with experimental validation," explicitly including "machine learning on chemical and biological data" and "the representation and computer-based searching of chemical databases." A methods-plus-evaluation paper on metabolite structure prediction is squarely in scope; the "experimental validation" clause is aimed at docking applications and does not bite here.

Article requirements that bear on this submission: ACS Research Data Policy **Level 2** — a Data Availability Statement is required at submission "describing the public availability of the data supporting the article's conclusions," with authors expected to "publicly share all the data underlying the results reported in the paper, preferably via archiving in an appropriate public repository." A TOC graphic is required (present, at 3.25 x 1.75 in and 300 dpi, with .tif/.eps supplied — compliant). Figure specs: colour 300 dpi, single column <=3.33 in, double column 4.167–7 in; colour must not be the only channel (Figure 1's lavender/green shading encodes the verdict and is described in the caption in words as well, which is the right pattern, though a redundant marker would be safer). Tables need a standalone one-phrase title — satisfied. SI needs a nonsentence per-file description with extensions — the SI paragraph is prose and lists content, not files with extensions; trivially fixable.

I read the recent JCIM neighbourhood to calibrate. Gao et al., *J. Chem. Inf. Model.* **2026**, 66, 2918–2928 (benchmarking SyGMa/GLORYx/BioTransformer/MetaPredictor/MetaTrans against human radiolabelled ADME data) is the closest comparator paper and is cited here as ref 14; it reports a coverage-versus-balanced-accuracy trade-off on 11 drugs and hedges accordingly. The AutoSOM paper (*JCIM* **2025**, 65, 7065) is the closest methods paper: 5,715 curated reactions, ChEMBL Structure Pipeline plus RDKit `CanonicalTautomer` for standardisation, and — the point for this submission — a ~4,000-word results section organised **by reaction chemistry** (addition 99.6%, elimination 94.7%, complex 78.8%; named handlers for glutathione conjugation, carnitine conjugation, ester hydrolysis) with an ablation showing performance plateaus after six named rules.

That is the standard of evidence this manuscript must meet, and it splits cleanly in two. On statistical evidence the submission is well **above** the JCIM norm — paired bootstrap intervals on every claim, a preregistration with falsification conditions, a criterion-by-budget sensitivity grid, declared populations, and an artifact-provenance sweep. I have not seen that discipline in this literature and it should be preserved. On **chemical** evidence it is below the norm: across the manuscript and SI the words "phase 1," "phase 2," "glucuronidation," "sulfation," "N-dealkylation," "hydroxylation," "CYP" and "epoxide" appear essentially nowhere (I grepped body.tex and si.tex: two incidental occurrences of "glutathione," one "deamination" in the worked example). A JCIM metabolism readership will not accept a 7,581-template rule bank characterised only as "4,417 distinct reaction types, where a type is the multiset of bonds that change between mapped atoms," nor a 475-metabolite coverage gap characterised only as "312 distinct types, of which 294 occur once."

Editorially: the two open brackets ([ZENODO DOI], [CORPUS LICENCE]) are normal pre-acceptance items, but the third — "[CORPUS ASSEMBLY: the per-source extraction queries and filters ... and the splitting algorithm and its seed]" — is a Level 2 problem rather than a placeholder, because the SI states plainly that without it "a reader can obtain the sources but cannot rebuild the triple files this work evaluates on." So is "[CURATED RULES: the published source, if any, of each of the four curated collections, and the licence each carries]," given that the rule bank is the released artifact and the paper's central object.

round1.summary:
GRAIL is a rule-bank plus learned-selector plus learned-filter metabolite-structure predictor, reported across five matching criteria and ten output budgets against every comparator that yields per-substrate predictions on 291 shared substrates. The evaluation contribution is real and, for this literature, unusually disciplined: leads are claimed only where a paired bootstrap interval excludes zero, no winner is declared, nine preregistered predictions are reported with three failures and three confirmations flagged as unresolved against their own intervals, and two boundary results (a 475/2,597 one-step coverage ceiling shown invariant across four definitions of a transformation type; 8.9% of mined templates derived from multi-piece reaction centres, which undercuts "single step") are reported against interest.

As the data, software and reproducibility referee my verdict is that the science is above the JCIM bar and the availability apparatus is below it. Four things block acceptance as submitted. (i) The Methods do not describe how the corpus was built: the SI carries "[CORPUS ASSEMBLY: the per-source extraction queries and filters, the structure standardisation, the cross-source de-duplication and conflict rule, the per-source counts, and the splitting algorithm and its seed]" and concedes "a reader can obtain the sources but cannot rebuild the triple files this work evaluates on." (ii) The Introduction's "the artifacts sufficient to recompute any cell are released" and the Discussion's "reproducible by a third party" are contradicted inside the paper's own SI, which states a third party can reproduce one of five criterion columns. (iii) The Zenodo deposit is unminted and held, and the deposit manifest the paper points readers to records 349 train and 293 validation substrates against a Data-and-Software-Availability sentence promising "every substrate of their population." (iv) 1,725 curated rules are redistributed with their published source and licence left as a placeholder, 492 of them from a collection "whose file is not in the repository," and the repository carries no licence for the code, checkpoints, harness or bank.

Beyond those, the leakage audit — the paper's central guarantee for its splits — is run at a single matching criterion, and it is the strictest of the five the paper itself declares, which is the exact failure mode the paper diagnoses in everyone else's work. Every one of the eight cross-document pointers from the main text into the SI names the wrong table, and one of them points at a table that does not contain the interval it cites. Comparator pinning is excellent for BioTransformer and absent for MetaTox and MetaPredictor. All of this is fixable in one round, most of it without new experiments; the leakage re-audit and the comparator-contamination audit are cheap re-runs over data the authors already hold.
round1.strengths:
The evaluation design is the contribution and it is a genuine one. Declaring the matching criterion and the output budget as axes and reporting the full 5x9 grid, rather than a cell, is the right diagnosis of why the numbers in this literature are not comparable, and Table S6 makes the case on the authors' own results: "At k = 15 the margin between GRAIL's better arm and the strongest comparator runs from -0.0692 under canonical SMILES equality to +0.0617 under the full InChIKey, a range of 0.1309, and the sign of the conclusion changes with it." The default criterion is shown to sit at the median of the five by number of budgets won — "The criterion this paper reports is not the one that flatters it" — which is the sort of thing authors normally leave to a referee to discover.

The statistical discipline holds throughout. Verdicts are read from paired bootstraps over substrates and from nothing else (Table S5), the multiple-comparisons exposure is stated rather than hidden ("The sweep is 9 budgets wide ... the narrowest lead we claim, at k = 30 against MetaTox, is the cell that would not survive such a correction"), and the paper declines to name a winner where the intervals do not support one.

Preregistration is used honestly. Of nine reported predictions three failed (P6 -0.1203, P7 -0.0286, P8 2.95x against a registered 10x) and are reported with mechanism; six of fifteen concern unreported work and are stated with thresholds so a later result cannot be a post hoc bar. P1, P2 and P5 are marked "unresolved rather than clear" because their registered threshold sits inside their own interval — I have not seen a JCIM Article do that.

Negative and limiting results are reported where they cost the authors something: SI S13's admission that an earlier ranking comparison "could not have answered" because 887 of 1,170 pools fit inside the budget; SI S12.1's disclosure that exact fusion ties at k=1 move recall by 0.0015; SI S11's disclosure that the typing artifact "is not byte-reproducible" with the drift quantified; the Limitations' concession that the coverage ceiling "is a one-template ceiling and not a one-enzyme one."

The licence analysis in SI S1 is more careful than most published corpora manage, and I checked it: DrugBank 5.1.x is indeed distributed under CC BY-NC 4.0 and ChEMBL 34 under CC BY-SA 3.0, and the incompatibility argument ("adding the non-commercial clause is a restriction ShareAlike does not permit, and dropping it breaches DrugBank's terms") is correct.

Comparator handling is candid where it can be. BioTransformer is pinned by jar digest rather than version string, with the reason given ("'3.0' names several builds"), and the reach figure is explicitly kept out of the recall table because "A reach figure and a ranked recall are not the same quantity." The four 2025-26 systems are reported as unrunnable with a per-system reason and a stated closing rule, and the contamination the corpus assembly creates is disclosed rather than buried: "No external evaluation set is reported, and the reason is the assembly rather than an audit finding."

Finally, the paper reports its own provenance hygiene against interest: "of 269 files under results/, 117 carry no stamp and 39 were written by a producer that has since changed."
round1.venue_notes:
JCIM (ACS), IF ~6.3-6.4, CiteScore 7.7, Q1, h-index 219; SciRev reports ~1.1 months to first decision, ~2.3 reports, 2.0 rounds, and reviewers rated 4.3/5 on report quality — a fast, serious, single-blind venue where a data/reproducibility referee's objections are normally actionable rather than fatal.

Scope: "publishes papers reporting new methodologies in chemical informatics and molecular modeling and its applications with experimental validation." A rule-grounded metabolite-structure predictor with a declared-axis evaluation is squarely in scope; JCIM has published MetaTox (2017), GLMCyp (2024), and Gao et al.'s "Benchmarking In Silico Metabolite Prediction Tools against Human Radiolabeled ADME Data" (2026, cited here as ref 14), so both the system and the benchmarking argument belong. Editorial guidance flags "submissions lacking data curation sections" as among those less likely to succeed — directly relevant below.

Article type: "Full-length research manuscripts" with no hard word limit; ~3,400-8,000 words and 8-17 journal pages is normal. At ~9,000 words over 17 pages this submission is at the upper end but within norm. TOC graphic present. Figure specs (300 dpi colour, 240 pt single / 300-504 pt double column, >=4.5 pt lettering) are not judgeable from the text extract but nothing renders anomalously in the PDF.

Data and software policy is the decisive part. JCIM applies **ACS Research Data Policy Level 2**: the journal "encourages all authors to publicly share all the data underlying the results reported in the paper, preferably via archiving in an appropriate public repository. Authors are required to provide a Data Availability Statement," which should carry "a means of access ... preferably through the use of a persistent identifier such as a DOI or an Accession Number." Level 2 does not make deposit a condition of publication (that is Level 3), so a candid statement of what is withheld is permitted — but the statement must be accurate.

The journal's own editorial on method and data sharing sets the substantive bar higher than Level 2's minimum: "For a work to be entirely reproducible, all data used must be accessible and all methods must be unambiguously described"; "data, including all molecular structures and their properties or activities, should be made available in a machine-readable format as Supporting Information or via a publicly available repository without infringements or restrictions. If more appropriate, scripts could be provided that extract the data used from freely available, public data sources"; "at least one data set used should be in the public domain or made available upon publication"; and "If it is not possible to release the source code for a new method, authors should provide a sufficient justification."

Two of those sentences bear directly. First, the extraction-script route is the exact escape hatch JCIM offers for a licence-encumbered corpus, and it is precisely what this submission's [CORPUS ASSEMBLY] placeholder withholds — so the paper's licence problem has a policy-sanctioned solution it has not taken. Second, releasing annotated metabolites only as hashes rather than structures is at odds with "all molecular structures ... in a machine-readable format," and the SI concedes the consequence.

Comparable recent JCIM metabolite work sets the practical standard: Ahlqvist et al.'s AstraZeneca MetID and SoM datasets were deposited to Zenodo with DOIs minted at publication (10.5281/zenodo.15319258, 10.5281/zenodo.15458630); AutoSOM (Jacob, Mazzolari, Kirchmair, JCIM 2025) ships an open-source tool with a GitHub link. Minted DOI plus a licensed repository is the norm here, not an aspiration. This submission has neither a minted DOI nor a licence.

SI format requirement: "A brief, nonsentence description of the actual contents of each file, including the file type extension, is required."

Net: the paper's evaluation discipline is above what JCIM currently publishes in this area — the Gao et al. benchmark it cites would have been improved by it. Its data and availability apparatus is below the bar, and mostly for reasons the authors can close in one revision cycle.

standing.claim: The Introduction's claim that the released artifacts suffice to recompute any cell is contradicted by the Supporting Information, and four load-bearing items of the Data Availability Statement are unresolved placeholders at submission.
standing.fix: Either resolve the placeholders before the revision is returned — mint the deposit, settle the licence position, publish the corpus assembly procedure and the curated-rule provenance — or withdraw the "recompute any cell" claim and replace it with a precise statement of which cells a third party can and cannot recompute, matching SI S1. If DrugBank's terms genuinely block redistribution of the derived corpus, say so in the main text as a limitation of the release rather than as a pending item, and consider releasing per-source rebuild scripts so a reader with their own DrugBank licence can reconstruct the splits and verify the manifest.

standing.claim: The 8.9% figure is not an upper bound on the composite share. It counts only reaction centres falling in disconnected pieces, and the paper's own worked example contains three composite templates whose centres are connected and therefore invisible to the instrument.
standing.fix: Re-describe 8.9% as the disconnected-centre share and stop calling it a bound on composites. Add a second instrument that catches connected composites — e.g. flag templates whose product side adds more than one instance of a recurring motif, or whose net change exceeds a plausible single-enzyme edit (I count 22 templates in the released bank that add two or more phosphorus atoms in one application, and 1,335 of 7,581 that graft five or more new mapped heavy atoms). Report the union. Then reconcile the revised composite share with the +0.012 depth-two result explicitly, because the two numbers are the same phenomenon seen twice.

I moved substantially. One of my four contested findings is withdrawn outright, two are conceded down from blocking, and one survives only after its mechanism was corrected — by the authors, against me. The recommendation band does not move, for reasons I set out at the end.

VENUE CALIBRATION. JCIM (IF ~6.4, Q1, ~1,100 articles/yr) publishes "new methodologies in chemical informatics ... and its application and validation"; its guidelines say papers "showing no advantage over existing methods" and papers "lacking data curation sections" are less likely to succeed, and it applies ACS Research Data Policy Level 2 (a Data Availability Statement describing public accessibility). Against the metabolite-prediction papers this journal actually prints — including its own ref 14 (Gao et al., JCIM 2026) and ref 5 (MetaTox, JCIM 2017) — the evaluation discipline here is well above the house standard. That is the frame for everything below.

=== FINDING 2 (selection optimism): WITHDRAWN. They are right and I was wrong. ===
I transported the wrong number. My arithmetic took the P1 optimism at k=15 on the uncapped pool (0.109 comparison minus 0.0733 validation = 0.0357) and set it against a k=30 lead on the deployed capped pool. SI Table S8 gives the budget-matched figures directly, and I recomputed them:
  k=30: fusion−product = 0.6391−0.5970 = +0.0421 (comparison, where selected); 0.6046−0.5710 = +0.0336 (validation); optimism = +0.0085. Lead over MetaTox at k=30 = 0.6391−0.6015 = +0.0376.
  k=50: optimism = 0.0241−0.0061 = +0.0180. Lead = 0.7038−0.6271 = +0.0767.
Both claimed leads clear the budget-matched optimism by a factor of four or more. Their estimator choice is also the correct one: a difference-in-differences on the same contrast across two populations, rather than a level comparison that would confound population difficulty. The finding is dead and I say so without reservation.

=== FINDING 1 (hydrogen convention / 475): CONCEDED DOWN, a residue remains. ===
Their refutation of the 460–688 range holds. I confirmed the docstring in scripts/engine_knobs.py:apply_with verbatim, and — more decisively — hydrogen_dispatch__clean_test.json itself records "legitimate_global_arms": ["all_implicit", "all_explicit_completed"], excluding the 0.7351 arm before I ever read it. I also found something that cuts further in their favour and that I had missed: coverage_gap_types.py:166 calls apply_with(mol, rules, False, "canonical", False) — add_hs=False — and preparation.py:362-370 states that every deployed firing path (ModelWrapper.generate, Generator.generate, factorized_infer) presents the molecule with hydrogens implicit. So the headline IS measured under the deployed convention, and among the legitimate arms it is the conservative end: 475 uncovered against 469 (explicit-completed) and 460 (per-rule dispatch). A bound chosen against the authors' own interest is not a selection defect.
What survives is smaller and still needs fixing. (a) The convention is named nowhere in either document — I grepped both; the only two hydrogen mentions are about BioTransformer's licence and the mining atom-flag list. Meanwhile the public entry point apply_rules_to_molecule defaults to DEFAULT_APPLICATION_PRESENTATION = "expanded", the other presentation, so a third party reproducing through the released API gets 0.7351/688, not 0.8171/475. One Methods sentence closes this. (b) The abstract's inference — "invariant to how a transformation type is defined, making it a property of the annotation corpus rather than of our implementation" — is licensed on the wrong axis. Type definition is a choice in the census of the gap, not in the engine. The authors' own dispatch artifact measures the engine axis and returns residual_convention_dependence 0.0035, CI [0.0015, 0.0058], excluding zero. Nine references in 2,597 changes no conclusion, but "rather than of our implementation" is exactly the class of overreach this paper's stated discipline forbids, and the instrument that would properly license a weaker version of the sentence is in their hands and uncited.

They are right about the standardiser and I was wrong. I ran grail_metabolism.utils.preparation.standardize_mol on both forms and on gemcitabine as drawn; all three collapse to Nc1ccn(C2OC(CO)C(O)C2(F)F)c(=O)n1. My stated mechanism is refuted.

So the corpus drawing reaches the matcher un-canonicalised and decides which rules fire. This is not copy-editing in this paper. === WHY THE BAND DOES NOT MOVE ===
The response is careful, checkable, and beat me twice on measurements I reproduced. That earns real credit, and the paper's core — the budget-and-criterion sweep, paired substrate bootstraps, registered predictions with three recorded failures reported as failures, the refusal to declare a winner, and the type-definition invariance on the ceiling — is above the JCIM bar and better disciplined than most metabolite-prediction work this journal prints. But two things keep it out of minor revision. First, the Data Availability Statement carries four unresolved bracketed items at submission, and the [CORPUS ASSEMBLY] one is not an author detail — it is a missing methods section (per-source queries, filters, standardisation, cross-source de-duplication and conflict rule, per-source counts, splitting algorithm and seed). Second, two of the remaining items require measurements the authors do not yet have — the second composite instrument they have agreed to build, and the substrate-presentation sweep — and the latter sits under the paper's only positive comparative claims. round2.reasoning:
I moved substantially on scope and not at all on the recommendation. Three of the four contested findings I withdraw outright; the fourth I do not, and the authors' own refutation is what enlarged it.

VENUE GROUNDING. JCIM Articles are full-length papers in chemical informatics with adequate validation; ACS Research Data Policy Level 2 requires a Data Availability Statement describing public availability of the data underlying the conclusions, preferably by repository deposit. The comparable recent JCIM work in this exact area — aweSOM (2025, 65, 8462), AutoSOM (2025, 65, 7065), EviCYP (2026, 66, 3892), and the GLORY/GLORYx/FAME line — reports recall at cut-offs on named populations and, without exception, spells out structure standardisation as a Methods step. That is the bar I am judging against.

WHAT I WITHDRAW

(1) The hydrogen-convention finding, as a blocker. The authors are right and I was wrong on the arithmetic that made it blocking. results/hydrogen_dispatch__clean_test.json — the artifact my own finding cited — carries the field legitimate_global_arms: ["all_implicit", "all_explicit_completed"], which disqualifies the all_explicit arm before I ever saw it. The defensible spread for the full bank on the 1,170-substrate evaluated test set is therefore 0.8163 (2,120 recovered) to 0.8229 (2,137, the per-template dispatch), i.e. 460–477 uncovered, not 460–688. The paper's \numCeilingCoverage = 0.8171 (2,122) sits essentially on the conservative implicit arm, which is guaranteed_reach — the number is not self-flattering. My "460 to 688" framing imported a documented incomplete loop as if it were a convention. Withdrawn. What survives is editorial: the convention is still named nowhere in manuscript or SI (I grepped both), and residual_convention_dependence is 0.0035 with CI [0.0015, 0.0058] excluding zero, so roughly 9–15 of the 98 "type held, rule did not fire" references are plumbing rather than chemistry. One sentence in Methods and a reconciliation of 0.8171 against the dispatch 0.8229.

(2) The selection-optimism finding. Refuted, and by my own error. Table S8 does carry the fusion-vs-product contrast to the comparison set AND the validation draw, on a fixed deployed pool, at k = 1, 5, 10, 15, 30, 50. At k = 15 the optimism is 0.0977 − 0.0504 = 0.0473; at k = 30, the budget of the only marginal head-to-head claim, it is 0.0421 − 0.0336 = 0.0085, against a lead over MetaTox of 0.6391 − 0.6015 = 0.0376. I transported a k=15 uncapped-pool number onto a k=30 deployed-pool claim, which is exactly the mismatch the paper flags in the paragraph I quoted. Withdrawn. Residual: Table S8 gives point estimates only, so the k=30 optimism is a difference of differences with no interval; add one.

(3) The SyGMa-containment finding, at blocking. My chemical identification was false. grail_metabolism/data/smirks.txt is 473 lines, not 474, and is not the SyGMa rule set. The real containment (results/bank_overlap_sygma.json: 152 of SyGMa's 175 verbatim inside extended_smirks.txt, 86.9% of SyGMa, 8.9% of GRAIL's curated half) is genuine and appears nowhere in the text. At JCIM, absorbing a published rule set is normal practice, not misconduct. One disclosed sentence — and it is an interesting one, because GRAIL contains 87% of SyGMa's rules and still trails it at k ≤ 5 with the interval excluding zero.

WHAT I DO NOT WITHDRAW, AND WHY IT GREW

(4) The tautomer axis. The authors refute my proposed mechanism and they are right about it: I reproduced their standardiser (RDKit 2024.09.6; Cleanup → FragmentParent → Uncharger → TautomerEnumerator.Canonicalize) and both gemcitabine forms collapse to Nc1ccn(C2OC(CO)C(O)C2(F)F)c(=O)n1, SDUQYLNIPVEERB. Standardisation does the reverse of what I said.

That demonstration convicts the worked example rather than clearing it.

  - results/case_study.json and results/case_study_exhaustive.json both record "substrate": "N=c1ccn(C2OC(CO)C(O)C2(F)F)c(O)n1". That is the 4-imino-2-hydroxy (lactim) tautomer. It is not gemcitabine, and it is not what the authors' own standardiser returns.
  - Rule 4913, [#7:1]:[#6:5](:[#7:4]:[#6:3](:[#6:2])=[#7:7])-[#8:6] >> ..., does NOT match gemcitabine as normally drawn (I tested both NC1=NC(=O)N(C=C1)[C@H]1O[C@H](CO)[C@@H](O)C1(F)F and the aromatic form: no match). It matches only the lactim form, yielding O=c1nc(O)ccn1... which standardises to dFdU, FIRDBEQIJQERSE. The reported firing atoms [0,1,2,4,15,16,17] include atom 16, the 2-OH oxygen, which exists only in the lactim.
  - Figure 2 prints that tautomer. At 900 dpi the base is unambiguous: exocyclic HO at C2 and exocyclic =NH at C4. A named drug is drawn wrongly in the paper's flagship figure.
  - Applying the whole bank to the correctly drawn substrate, all four references are still reached — dFdU via rules 234, 251, 305, 2199, 4483, and the three phosphates via 1745, 2198, 2139. So "4 of 4 found" survives. What does not survive is every rule attribution in Table 3 and Figure 2 for dFdU, the ranks (8/13/16/21), and hence the per-molecule 0.50@15 and 1.00@30. The interactive arm's single hit is the most fragile of all, since its 30-rule selection was made on the lactim.

This is not one figure. In results/label_convention_audit.json — whose own note says these are the substrates MolFrame.label_reactions applies rules to — 55 of 150 corpus substrates (36.7%) are not fixed points of the paper's declared standardiser, and every one of the 55 differences is a pure tautomer move (identical molecular formula; zero formula changes). 31 of 150 carry an explicit N=C(O)/C(O)=N iminol, i.e. amides written as imidic acids: an erlotinib–glutathione conjugate with both peptide bonds as iminol; an acetamide as N=C(C)O; a Boc carbamate as N=C(O)OC(C)(C)C; a macrocyclic HCV-protease-inhibitor-like substrate with amide, carbamate and acylsulfonamide all iminol.

It propagates into the bank. Parsing all 7,580 parseable templates, 741 (9.8%) require an iminol carbon C(=N)–O on the reactant side — 681 of the 5,866 mined (11.6%) and 60 of the 1,715 curated (3.5%). That is more templates than require the real amide motif C(=O)–N (714, 9.4%). Amide hydrolysis and amide N-dealkylation are core phase-I chemistry. A bank in which the unpopulated iminol outnumbers the amide is not a bank a working metabolism chemist can read or reuse.

Because substrate and reference share the dialect, the recall numbers are internally valid and I am not claiming they are wrong. But three things break:
  - The paper's own stated discipline that "the evaluation criterion and the output budget are declared axes, not defaults." The tautomer dialect of the INPUT is a third axis. The paper sweeps five ways of judging a hit; it never names or sweeps how the substrate is drawn.
  - "Populations are named and never mixed": the worked example's population of one is not the molecule it is named as.
  - The transferability claim, which is the paper's chemistry selling point — "a user reading the output sees which transformation is claimed and where, and can reject a candidate on chemical grounds." A chemist who draws gemcitabine, or any amide-bearing drug, the way every database and drawing program does will not exercise ~10% of the bank and will not reproduce the showcase.

And it lands precisely on an existing open item: SI S1 says how the four sources were "queried, filtered, standardised, de-duplicated ... and split" is [CORPUS ASSEMBLY: ...], a placeholder. The undocumented step is the one that produced this.

ABOVE OR BELOW THE BAR. The evaluation contribution is above JCIM's bar and comfortably so — the declared-axes sweep, paired bootstraps over substrates, registered predictions with thresholds tested off the selection population, the honest refusal to name a winner, and the reported failures (P6, P7, P8) are better discipline than most of what this journal publishes in metabolite prediction. The generated-macro/pinned-artifact apparatus is genuinely unusual and worth keeping. But a JCIM Article that prints a named drug as a minor tautomer in its flagship figure, and attributes its one interactive-mode hit to a rule that provably cannot fire on that drug, will draw a correction after publication. That is fixable, not fatal. Major revision stands — narrowed to two accepted items, three one-sentence additions, and one real piece of chemistry work.

WHAT THE RESPONSE CHANGED

The two admissible arms recover 2,120 and 2,128 of 2,597, i.e. 469–477 uncovered against a reported 475. "460 to 688" was not a menu of conventions; it was two defensible arms plus one the code documents as an incomplete loop. What survives is a naming defect, not a selection defect. WHAT IT DID NOT CHANGE

1. The remedy for my own finding is a disjunction whose second branch is a relabeling. The response offers: resolve the placeholders, OR withdraw the "recompute any cell" claim and state precisely which cells can and cannot be recomputed. The second branch leaves the hole and renames it. The hole is [CORPUS ASSEMBLY] — the per-source extraction queries and filters, the standardisation, the cross-source de-duplication and conflict rule, the per-source counts, and the splitting algorithm and its seed. That is not a fact the authors are waiting on; it is the Methods subsection describing how the instrument the whole paper is about was built, and they necessarily possess it. The SI states the consequence plainly: a reader "can obtain the sources but cannot rebuild the triple files this work evaluates on, and the split manifest can only prove that a rebuilt corpus differs, not how." No licence blocks a procedure. AutoSOM put its curation in SI; this paper has a bracket where that section goes. Branch one is required for this item.

2. The cover note misdescribes two of the four brackets and contradicts the authors' own accept-text. The note says "The bracketed values are author information and a licence determination, not measurements." [CORPUS ASSEMBLY] is neither. [CURATED RULES] — "the published source, if any, of each of the four curated collections, and the licence each carries" — is half provenance, and covers 1,725 of 7,581 templates that the SI tells readers to "treat as unattributed". I confirmed the shortfall is real: data/smirks.txt (474), data/merged_smirks.txt (656) and resources/notebooks_rules.txt (1,051) are present and deduplicate to 1,233; the remaining 492 come from a collection with no file in the repository. The response's own numbered accept-text gets this right — it promises "the corpus assembly procedure and the curated-rule provenance". The closing note walks it back. I hold the authors to the accept-text. An editor reading only the note would pass the paper with two substantive gaps recast as clerical ones.

3. [ZENODO DOI] is severable from the licence question and resolvable today. Zenodo reserves a DOI on an unpublished draft precisely so it can be printed in a manuscript; the record registers only on publication. The authors' stated blocker — that a published record cannot be withdrawn — does not apply to a reserved DOI. Reserve, print, publish at acceptance. This is the ordinary route and it costs nothing, so it should not sit in the list of items called genuinely unresolved.

4. The SyGMa containment is not editorial, and the rebuttal does not reach it. The authors concede results/bank_overlap_sygma.json: 152 of SyGMa's 175 rules verbatim in the bank, appearing nowhere in the paper. They then rebut by showing data/smirks.txt is not the SyGMa rule set. That rebuts which file, not whether. Their own artifact settles the load-bearing part: in_grail_curated_subset: 152, in_grail_mined_subset: 0. All 152 sit in the curated half — the half the SI declares unattributed. On the authors' own figures at most 75 are in data/smirks.txt, so the balance lies in merged_smirks.txt, notebooks_rules.txt, or the 492-rule collection with no file. The containment measurement is therefore evidence bearing on the missing collection's origin, and the authors already hold it: it is a partial answer to [CURATED RULES] that the paper declines to give. It is also an attribution question — a bank containing 86.9% of SyGMa's rules verbatim is to that extent a derivative carrying SyGMa's terms — and a comparison question, since a reader meeting "SyGMa ahead at k<=5, GRAIL ahead at k=30 and k=50" is entitled to know beforehand that the two arms are not independent.

5. New, and arising from the response itself: the rebuttal's evidence is held to a lower standard than the paper's. The stated discipline is that every number on the page comes from a pinned artifact and a checker refuses any literal that does not. That discipline was not applied to the reply. results/bank_overlap_sygma.json — the artifact cited to concede the containment, whose 86.9% the authors propose to add to the text — is unstamped in their own sweep ("no provenance block: nothing records which code wrote this"); it is one of the 117. results/hydrogen_dispatch__clean_test.json, the source of the 0.7351/0.8163/0.8194 arms carrying the hydrogen rebuttal, is not in the provenance registry at all, neither pinned nor swept. ceiling_convention_matched.json is producer_unknown ("commit a227873afa32 does not carry scripts/ceiling_convention_matched.py"); convention_census.json is unstamped; contraction_choice.json is producer_unknown. This does not make the rebuttals wrong — I checked the hydrogen arithmetic and it is internally consistent, and the containment number matches its file. But it has a hard consequence: every number the response proposes to add to the paper must be regenerated under a stamped producer first, or the checker that is part of what the authors are offering will refuse the literal. Relaxing the checker to admit them would cost the paper the apparatus that most distinguishes it.

WHY MAJOR AND NOT MINOR

Everything in my own lane is a writing task. No new experiment closes it, and on the data, software and reproducibility axis alone I would move to minor revision — the release is above the venue norm, the apparatus verifies, and the remaining items are sections the authors can write from what they already have. I stay at major for two reasons visible from where I sit. First, the composite-template finding the authors themselves accepted as major requires a new instrument for connected composites, a union with the 8.9% disconnected-centre share, and a reconciliation with the +0.012 depth-two result: that is new measurement re-deriving a limitation the Discussion currently states as a bound. Second, the SyGMa disclosure has been scoped as one sentence when it is simultaneously a Methods disclosure, a comparison caveat, and a partial resolution of the curated-rule provenance. A revision carrying both is a major revision in ACS's ordinary sense, whatever my own conditions have narrowed to.

Sources consulted for venue grounding: ACS Research Data Policy (https://researcher-resources.acs.org/publish/data_policy); JCIM Author Guidelines (https://researcher-resources.acs.org/publish/author_guidelines?coden=jcisd8); AutoSOM, JCIM 2025 (https://pubs.acs.org/jcisd8/article/65/13/7065/3687688/Automated-Annotation-of-Sites-of-Metabolism-from); Zenodo DOI reservation (https://support.zenodo.org/help/en-gb/1-upload-deposit/35-how-can-i-reserve-a-doi-before-i-publish).

editor.letter_to_authors:
Dear Authors,

Re: "Rule-grounded metabolite prediction under a fully declared evaluation" — Article, JCIM

Three referees have reported, you have responded, and all three have reported again. All three arrive at major revision. So do I, and I have satisfied myself independently of the reasons rather than averaging their recommendations. This letter records what I checked myself, what is now settled, what stands, and what I am asking for.

WHERE I STAND ON THE PAPER

The evaluation contribution is real and it is above what this journal prints in this subfield. Declaring the matching criterion and the output budget as axes and reporting the full grid rather than a cell is the correct diagnosis of why the recall figures in metabolite prediction are not comparable, and Table S6 proves it on your own numbers rather than about somebody else's: the margin at k=15 runs from -0.0692 to +0.0617 and the sign of the conclusion moves with the criterion. Reporting that your default criterion sits at the median of five by budgets won, refusing to order systems by precision and then printing precision because it orders them differently, reporting three registered predictions as failures with their mechanisms, marking three of six confirmations "unresolved rather than clear" because the threshold sits inside the interval, disclosing the molecular overlap and the contamination that flatters your comparators, and stating that 117 of 269 files under results/ carry no stamp and support no number — I do not often see any one of these, and I have not before seen them together in a submission to this journal. Section S13's rule, that a ranking comparison carries information only over substrates whose pool exceeds the budget, is a methodological result this literature needs and it came out of your own failed experiment.

I want that on the record before the conditions, because the conditions are substantial and I do not want them read as a verdict on the work.

WHAT IS NOW SETTLED, AND WHAT YOU CAN STOP WORKING ON

Your response was disciplined and it beat two referees on measurements those referees then reproduced and conceded. Specifically:

The selection-optimism finding is dead. Both referees who raised it withdrew it in full. Your estimator choice — a difference-in-differences on the same contrast across two populations — is the right one, and the budget-matched optimism at k=30 (+0.0085) against a lead of +0.0376 is not close. Do not spend revision effort here.

The "460 to 688" hydrogen range is dead as a blocking finding. I confirmed that hydrogen_dispatch__clean_test.json itself records legitimate_global_arms as ["all_implicit", "all_explicit_completed"], excluding the 0.7351 arm before any referee read the file. The admissible band is 0.8163 to 0.8229, and your reported 0.8171 sits essentially on guaranteed_reach — the conservative end. A bound chosen against your own interest is not a selection defect and I will not treat it as one.

The claim that data/smirks.txt is the SyGMa rule set is dead. You refuted it and the referee withdrew it.

WHAT STANDS, INCLUDING THINGS I CHECKED MYSELF

1. The worked example is wrong, and your own refutation is what establishes it. You are right that standardize_mol does not create a minor tautomer — I ran it, and both the drawn 4-amino-2-oxo form and the 4-imino-2-hydroxy form collapse to Nc1ccn(C2OC(CO)C(O)C2(F)F)c(=O)n1. That is precisely the problem. results/case_study.json records the substrate as N=c1ccn(C2OC(CO)C(O)C2(F)F)c(O)n1 — the lactim. If your standardiser would have canonicalised it and the pipeline did not, then the substrate reached the matcher un-standardised, exactly as drawn in the corpus. I then tested rule 4913 directly: its reactant side requires the exocyclic imine, and it does not match gemcitabine as normally drawn in either the Kekulé or the aromatic form. It matches only the lactim. Figure 2 therefore prints a named drug as a minor tautomer, and Table 3 attributes the interactive mode's only hit to a rule that cannot fire on the molecule the caption names. The refutation of the mechanism convicts the example rather than clearing it.

2. It is not one figure. I ran the corpus substrates in results/label_convention_audit.json through your own declared standardiser: 56 of 150 are not fixed points of it, and 34 of 150 carry an explicit iminol N=C–O — amides written as imidic acids. It propagates into the bank. Parsing the released templates, I count 726 requiring an iminol C(=N)–O on the reactant side against 702 requiring a real amide C(=O)–N. A bank in which the unpopulated tautomer of the amide outnumbers the amide is not a bank a working metabolism chemist can read or reuse, and amide hydrolysis and amide N-dealkylation are core phase-I chemistry.

I want to be exact about what this does and does not damage. Because substrate and reference share the dialect, your recall figures are internally valid and I am not asking you to defend them. The referee's check that the exhaustive arm still reaches 4 of 4 on the correctly drawn molecule suggests the qualitative conclusion survives. What does not survive is the flagship figure, the rule attributions and ranks in Table 3 and Table S9, the per-molecule recalls, and — by your own thesis — the claim that every evaluation choice is declared. The tautomer dialect of the input is an axis. You sweep five ways of judging a hit and never name how the substrate is drawn. It also lands on your transferability claim, which is the paper's chemistry selling point: a chemist who draws an amide-bearing drug the way every database draws it will not exercise roughly a tenth of your bank.

3. The SyGMa containment is not editorial. I read results/bank_overlap_sygma.json: 152 of SyGMa's 175 rules verbatim inside the bank, 86.9% of SyGMa, all 152 in the curated half and 0 in the mined half. This appears nowhere in the manuscript or the SI, while you disclose the opposite-direction contamination that flatters your comparators, twice and unprompted. Absorbing a published rule set is normal practice and nobody here is suggesting otherwise. But a reader meeting "SyGMa ahead at k≤5, GRAIL ahead at k=30 and k=50" is entitled to know beforehand that the two arms are not independent, and the honest reading of Figure 1 changes: SyGMa's head-of-list lead becomes a ranking result on largely shared chemistry, and your depth advantage becomes that bank plus 7,429 further templates. Two further things make this more than a caveat. All 152 sit in the half your SI tells readers to treat as unattributed, so the measurement is a partial answer to [CURATED RULES] that you already hold and decline to give. And a bank containing 86.9% of SyGMa's rules verbatim is to that extent a derivative — an attribution question in a paper that is otherwise scrupulous about licences.

4. [CORPUS ASSEMBLY] is a missing methods section, not a pending value. I checked the JCIM author guidelines directly. The journal applies ACS Research Data Policy Level 2, and it names "manuscripts lacking data curation sections" among the categories less likely to succeed. That is a house criterion, not a referee preference. Your own SI states the consequence: a reader "can obtain the sources but cannot rebuild the triple files this work evaluates on." No licence blocks a procedure. Your cover note describes the four brackets as "author information and a licence determination, not measurements"; that is accurate for two of them and not for this one or for [CURATED RULES], and your own numbered accept-text gets it right where the closing note walks it back. I am holding you to the accept-text. The disjunction you offered — resolve the placeholders OR restate precisely which cells can be recomputed — is acceptable for the licence question and is not acceptable here. Branch one is required.

5. Every cross-reference from the main text into the SI is wrong. I checked all of them against the SI's own table order. Eight in the manuscript (body lines pointing at S6, S2, S4, S4, S1, S3, and the captions of Tables 2 and 4) and one internal to the SI ("the tautomer column of Table S4"). Nine pointers, nine wrong, none right. In most papers this is copy-editing. Not in this one. It has already caused measurable harm: it is the direct cause of the referee finding that was raised, argued at length, and then withdrawn — the wrong pointer sent him to the criterion table when the deployed-pool contrast lives in the ranking grid. And it falsifies, as written, your response's closing claim that "every numerical claim in the paper reaches the page from a pinned artifact through a generated macro, and a checker refuses any numeric literal that does not." Nine typed literals reached the page and all nine are wrong. The apparatus you are offering as the answer to the referees' concerns has a hole exactly at the referee's entry point.

6. The composite instrument, which you accepted. One statistical condition on the remedy, which I am adopting from the methods referee because it is correct: pre-specify the second instrument's threshold before running it. The candidates in your response (≥2 added phosphorus; ≥5 new mapped heavy atoms, 1,335 of 7,581) were chosen after seeing the first result. Register the threshold the way P1–P9 were registered, or the union you report is a forking path in a paper built to prevent them.

7. Two claims in the front matter overreach. The Introduction's "the artifacts sufficient to recompute any cell are released" is contradicted by SI S1 and must go. The abstract's "invariant to how a transformation type is defined, making it a property of the annotation corpus rather than of our implementation" is licensed on the wrong axis: type definition is a choice in the census of the gap, not in the engine. Your own hydrogen_dispatch artifact measures the engine axis and returns residual_convention_dependence 0.0035, CI [0.0015, 0.0058], which excludes zero. Nine references in 2,597 changes no conclusion, and that is exactly why the sentence should be corrected rather than defended — it is the one class of overreach your stated discipline forbids, and the instrument that would license a weaker, true version of it is in your hands.

ONE OBSERVATION THAT MAY SAVE YOU WORK

Conditions 1, 2 and 3 are one defect seen three times. The undocumented standardisation step inside corpus assembly is what produced the stored dialect; the dialect is what put a lactim in your flagship figure; and the mined templates, derived from those drawings, are what inverted the iminol/amide ratio in the bank. Writing [CORPUS ASSEMBLY] honestly will force you through the other two. I would do it first and let the rest fall out, rather than treating them as three chores.

TWO THINGS I WILL NOT ASK FOR

I am not asking that the leads survive condition 3. If canonicalising substrates before application narrows or erases the k=30 and k=50 margins, that is a result and the paper reports it; you already decline to name a winner and the paper has room to absorb it. The revision will be judged on whether the axis is declared and measured, not on which way it comes out. Setting the other condition would be the precise defect this paper exists to criticise.

And I am not asking you to trim any disclosure. Under revision pressure authors routinely cut exactly the material three referees praised here — the molecular overlap counts, the 117-unstamped admission, the reported failures, the "3 of 5" line, the S13 self-invalidation. Keep all of it. The two disclosures I am adding, SyGMa containment and substrate presentation, make the paper stronger by its own standard rather than weaker.

PROCESS

The conditions below are binding. Conditions 1 through 3 require work you do not yet have and will return to the chemistry and reproducibility referees; the remainder I can assess myself. Nothing found in two rounds reverses a stated conclusion of the paper, which is why this is a revision and not a rejection, and why I expect to publish it. Please return a point-by-point response in the same style as your first — it was checkable, it was right twice against referees who then verified and conceded, and it is the reason I am confident this paper can be closed in one more round.

Yours sincerely,
Handling Editor, Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

editor.standing_at_this_journal:
Publishable here, and I expect to publish it — but as an evaluation-methodology paper, not as a leaderboard result, which is what it says of itself and is to its credit.

Against what JCIM actually prints in this subfield — MetaTox (JCIM 2017), Gao et al.'s radiolabelled-ADME benchmark (JCIM 2026), AutoSOM (JCIM 2025), aweSOM (2025), the GLORY/GLORYx/FAME line — the evaluation discipline is well above the house standard, and on several axes I have not seen it here at all. Declared axes with the full 5x9 grid reported rather than a chosen cell; paired substrate bootstraps as the sole basis for every verdict; a preregistration with three failures reported as failures and three confirmations marked unresolved against their own intervals; an explicit refusal to name a winner; and a pinned-artifact provenance system with a numeral checker. I have not previously handled a JCIM metabolite-prediction Article that reported its own registered failures, and Table S6 alone — where the sign of the conclusion flips between canonical SMILES and full InChIKey at k=15 — is the sort of table that changes how referees in this area read every subsequent recall figure. That is where this paper's citations will come from, and I would expect it to be cited more for the evaluation apparatus than for GRAIL.

The release position is also above the operative bar, contrary to my reproducibility referee's first-round view, which he withdrew after checking the comparator: the closest recent JCIM paper in this space ships a bare GitHub link, a co-author-owned primary dataset, no repository DOI and no licence analysis. This submission releases source, both checkpoints, the bank, a digest-pinned split manifest, frozen per-substrate comparator predictions, the harness and the preregistration, plus an account of what cannot be rebuilt. ACS Level 2 requires a Data Availability Statement, not code deposit; the gap is the unfilled brackets, not the ambition.

The chemistry presentation is currently below house standard, and that is the whole of the distance to acceptance. Every comparable paper in this line spells out structure standardisation as a Methods step; this one has a bracket where that section goes, and the consequence is visible in the flagship figure, where a named drug is drawn as a minor tautomer and its one interactive-mode hit is attributed to a rule that cannot fire on the correctly drawn structure. Published as submitted, that draws a correction. It is also entirely fixable, and the fix is bounded: I verified the recall numbers are internally valid because substrate and reference share the dialect, and nothing found across two rounds reverses a stated conclusion.

On the journal's own stated grounds for rejection, one applies and one does not. "Manuscripts lacking data curation sections" applies squarely and is why condition 1 is binding. "Models without advantages over existing methods" does not: leads at k=30 and k=50 with intervals excluding zero are demonstrated, the budget-matched selection optimism is an order below them, and the methodological contribution stands on its own. The SyGMa disclosure sharpens that question without answering it against the paper — "the same rules plus 7,429 more, ranked" is still an advantage, and stating it plainly is better for the paper than having a reader discover it.

Risk assessment for the next round: low. The authors demonstrated across the first round that they check claims properly against artifacts and concede cleanly when wrong — they beat two referees on measurements those referees then reproduced and withdrew, which is a better signal about a group's standards than any single result in the paper. My residual concern is not competence but scope: condition 3 could narrow the head-to-head margins, and I have pre-committed in the letter that this will not count against them, so that they are not tempted to design the measurement toward a preferred answer. If conditions 1 through 3 come back honestly done, this is an accept.

all_findings.where: Section 1, final paragraph; Section 7 "Data and software availability"; SI Section S1

all_findings.where: Section 2.1 "Which population carries which number"; Figure 1 caption; Table 2 caption; SI Section S14

all_findings.where: Section 4.2 ("Every prediction names the transformation rule that produced it and the site at which it fired, so a user can accept or reject a candidate on chemical grounds"); Table 3; Table S9

all_findings.where: Section 3.11 and Figure 4; Section 4.4; Table 5
all_findings.claim: The 475-metabolite coverage gap — the paper's second headline result — is never characterised chemically. The reader is told it comprises "312 distinct types, of which 294 occur once" and nothing about what chemistry is missing.

For the 98 known-type misses, say what blocks them — my reading of the one-bond expansion is that the environment is over-specified, and "relaxing the convention-dependent primitives recovers three" suggests you have already begun this diagnosis. This single addition would do more for the paper's usefulness to its readership than any further statistics.

The second is the stronger paper and looks inexpensive given the tooling already in place.

If the answer is few, that is a genuinely strong result and materially strengthens the ADME-mining argument; if many, the paper has found the extension it recommends.

all_findings.claim: GLORYx is not a comparator, and no reason is given. It is open source, runnable, produces ranked output with priority scores, and is the closest published system in design to GRAIL.

If there is a reason it cannot be run, state it in S17 alongside the other four, under the same rule. Consider also reporting the GLORYx and SyGMa rule sets' one-step reach on your test substrates next to your bank's 0.8171, which is the natural chemistry control for whether 7,581 mined templates buy reach over ~150–400 curated ones.

Report a quality census of the bank: how many templates are chemically well formed (map-consistent, net change compatible with a plausible single enzymatic edit), how many are conjugations, and what the distribution of new-mapped-atom counts looks like. all_findings.where: Section 2.1 and SI S1; Data and software availability; SI S6 (butyrylthiocholine)
all_findings.claim: No chemical audit of the 2,597 test references is reported, and two defects are visible in passing: two substrates carry their own key among their references, and the thiol and thiolate of butyrylthiocholine are annotated as separate metabolites.

all_findings.where: Data and software availability; SI S1 ([CORPUS ASSEMBLY]); SI S7 ("7,580 parse under RDKit 2022.09.5")
all_findings.claim: Three reproducibility items sit below ACS Research Data Policy Level 2 as submitted, over and above the two acknowledged placeholders.
